checkpoints: In NestJS, guards registered inside @UseGuards run strictly in the order they are listed, not in whatever order seems logically sensible — so @UseGuards(RolesGuard, JwtAuthGuard) actually executes RolesGuard first, before JwtAuthGuard ever runs.

RolesGuard reads req.user.role, but req.user is only ever populated by JwtAuthGuard after it verifies the Bearer token — so if RolesGuard runs before JwtAuthGuard, req.user is undefined for every single request regardless of what the client sends.

Because req.user is always undefined in this ordering, RolesGuard's check `!role || !requiredRoles.includes(role)` evaluates to true unconditionally and throws ForbiddenException for every caller — a valid admin token, a wrong-role token, and a missing token all collapse into the identical 403 response.

A request with no token at all never reaches JwtAuthGuard — the guard responsible for returning 401 on missing or invalid credentials — because RolesGuard short-circuits first with 403; the two symptoms (valid admin token still 403, and no token also 403 instead of 401) are two faces of the same misordering, not two separate bugs.

The underlying invariant is authentication before authorization: identity must be attached to the request (or the request rejected with 401) before any role or permission check can run, since authorization has nothing valid to compare against otherwise.

The fix is to swap the guard order to @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard), so JwtAuthGuard verifies the token and attaches req.user first — throwing 401 itself if the token is missing or invalid — and only then does RolesGuard compare the real req.user.role against the declared @Roles allow-list.

401 and 403 carry distinct meanings for client behavior: 401 means the caller is not authenticated and should re-login, while 403 means the caller is authenticated but not permitted and should not retry with the same credentials — running authorization before authentication collapses both into 403 and can mislead client retry logic.

The fix should be verified and locked in with a three-call status-code matrix — admin token → 200, valid token with the wrong role → 403, no token → 401 — kept as a regression test so a future guard-reordering mistake fails a test loudly instead of shipping silently.
